name: Buffalo
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: The buffalo is a triple-purpose animal: milk, draught work and good meat. It turns ordinary fodder and crop by-products into meat better than cows, and in countries like Italy, Bulgaria, Egypt and the Philippines fattened buffaloes gain more than 1 kg a day. Pakistan had about 34.6 million buffaloes (Economic Survey 2014), and about 50 percent of the country's meat comes from buffaloes. Research shows big room for improvement in breeding, feeding, care and disease control. Canal areas with wheat, sugarcane, cotton, maize and rice give plenty of by-products for feed, and canals, rivers and marshes give buffaloes water to wallow in, which suits their nature.
aspects.breeds:
Nili: from the Sutlej valley (Mailsi in Vehari, and Pakpattan); named after the blue (nila) water of the Sutlej. Mostly black, some brown; small strong head, curved pointed horns, long neck, tail almost touching the ground, short legs, teats about 20 cm long. Gives 10 to 15 kg of milk a day.
Ravi: from the Ravi valley, Sandal Bar (around Okara, Kamalia, Samundri, Tandlianwala, Chichawatni), and a few along the Chenab in Gujrat and Jhang. Black or brown; bigger head than Nili, short thick neck, broad back, heavy body, long teats, coiled drooping horns. Gives 8 to 14 kg a day.
Panch kalyan: Nili or Ravi animals with white lower legs, forehead, tail switch, chin and inner eyes, prized for looks.
Nili-Ravi: the two breeds have mixed so pure animals are rare; today's Punjab buffalo is Nili-Ravi. First calving at about 1,390 days, lactation about 322 days, about 2,430 litres per lactation (some give 3,000 to 5,000 litres), about 7.5 litres a day, calving interval about 512 days, dry period about 190 days.
Kundi: from Larkana, Hyderabad, Nawabshah and Sukkur (Sindh); short curved horns like a fish hook (kundi). Heavy black body, shorter legs, soft skin, thin tail. First calving at about 1,640 days, lactation about 325 days, about 2,215 litres per lactation, about 6.8 litres a day, calving interval about 512 days.
Selecting animals: judge both appearance and hidden potential. Body weight, length and chest and belly girth explain about 12.3 percent of milk yield; each extra inch of belly girth adds about 0.31 kg of milk a day. Milk ability is inherited, so compare mothers' and daughters' records. Progeny testing (ranking bulls by their daughters' milk) is the most reliable way to choose bulls.
aspects.breeding:
Puberty: Nili-Ravi at about 3 years, Kundi at about 3.5 years; better feeding and care can lower this. Feeding concentrate to young heifers brings heat earlier and can give one extra calving in a lifetime.
Heat (bahar): heat signs last 3 to 69 hours, about 20 hours on average, and only about 24 percent of buffaloes show clear signs (silent heat). Heat is strongest after sunset, peaks at midnight and is weakest around noon. Signs fade after about 18 hours in heifers and 22 hours in buffaloes; ovulation starts as signs disappear, which is the best time for mating or insemination.
Fertility rarely goes above 70 to 72 percent even with good care. Causes: poor management, unbalanced feed, wrong timing of insemination, genetics and reproductive diseases. Uterine infection was found in about 37.8 percent of problem buffaloes and 27.5 percent of heifers; small or inactive ovaries in 8.9 and 13.8 percent; cystic ovaries in about 5 percent.
Breeding: use artificial insemination where available. If you must use natural mating, use a bull with a known production record; government livestock farms sell recorded bull calves. Bahadurnagar (Okara) has worked on buffalo improvement since 1984, and a buffalo research institute at Bhunikey, Pattoki, records private buffaloes to select bull mothers.
Brucellosis (contagious abortion) causes abortion between the 5th and 7th month of pregnancy; vaccinate, keep strict hygiene and avoid natural mating where possible.
aspects.care:
Milking buffaloes: heat and humidity cut milk badly, so bathe them twice a day in summer. In a Bahadurnagar study (June to December), buffaloes kept under shade trees ate more and gave more milk than those in sheds with fans or with fans and water sprays.
Pregnant buffaloes need plenty of feed: they maintain their body, make milk and grow the calf; underfeeding gives weak calves and less milk. Three or four days before and after calving give lukewarm drinking water and easily digested, laxative feed, and protect from harsh weather. Near calving keep her in a separate clean, disinfected room with a thick layer of rice straw on the floor. Don't interfere with the birth; call a vet if needed.
Suckling calves: about 40 percent of calf deaths come from stomach and intestine diseases, mostly due to wrong feeding. Give colostrum (bohli, the first 3 days' milk) at one tenth of body weight a day, in 2 to 3 feeds 8 hours apart; it protects against disease. Letting calves suckle the mother directly often gives too much milk and white scours. Experts recommend separating calves 3 days after birth and feeding with a bucket or nipple; train buffaloes to let down milk without the calf. Give milk at body temperature (calves are 37.7 °C), diluting slightly with water if needed. Milk only until one month, then add good green fodder, grass or concentrate; nursing age is about 3 months. A muzzle after feeding and pucca floors stop calves licking soil; individual pens stop them eating soil and hair. Wash feeding pails with washing soda and dry in the sun.
Health basics: fresh water and full, balanced, tasty feed; suitable temperature and fresh air in the shed; good light; and prompt diagnosis and treatment. Signs of illness: less appetite, less milk, no cud chewing, dull coat, red eye membranes, dry muzzle, flared nostrils, frothing, difficult breathing, restless eyes, slow or staggering walk, drooping ears.
Disinfection: sun, heat and fresh air are the best natural disinfectants; chemicals include chlorine, iodine, lime, washing soda, caustic soda, potassium permanganate, phenyl, Dettol, Lysol and cresol. Wash shed floors daily and spray 2 percent phenyl or another disinfectant.
aspects.shed: Build the shed on ground higher than its surroundings; low sheds collect rainwater, can collapse and spread disease. Plant shade trees around it. Run the length east–west so sunlight reaches inside in every season, keeping it dry and germ-free. Each buffalo needs 40 square feet covered and twice that open: 25 buffaloes need a 1,000 square foot shed (25 x 40 or 20 x 50 feet) with a 2,000 square foot yard; the same space holds twice as many young stock over a year old. Shed height 10 feet. Keep it cheap but durable: brick walls on three sides, pillars in front, T-iron and asbestos sheet roof; close gaps between pillars with sacking or chiks in winter. Build separate sheds for the bull, dry buffaloes, heifers and suckling calves, plus a store, a milk room and a chaff-cutter room.
aspects.feed:
Green fodder: about 10 percent of body weight, 40 to 70 kg per buffalo a day. Fodder is most nutritious just before flowering, and animals like it best then. Dry fodder (wheat straw, rice straw, dry grass) is used all year; surplus sorghum, maize, oats or millet can be dried and stored for shortage periods without losing nutrition.
Needs differ for milking, dry, pregnant buffaloes, heifers and calves. Milking buffaloes need enough protein, calcium and phosphorus, which go out in the milk; pregnant ones need calcium. Draught animals need energy and fat; fattening calves need plenty of grain.
Many farmers feed concentrate (wanda) only to milking animals, but feeding it to young heifers brings earlier puberty, and feeding it in pregnancy gives heavier, healthier calves. Feeding concentrate by need raises milk and shortens the calving interval.
Cheap by-products can replace costly cottonseed cake: blood, molasses, sugarcane bagasse, bone meal/DCP, rice polish, wheat bran, maize gluten, guar meal, fish meal, urea, cottonseed and toria meal, sunflower meal, wheat straw, rice straw and mustard cake. Urea (40 percent nitrogen) can be used at 1 to 2 percent of concentrate without harm, or sprayed on wheat or rice straw as a 4 percent solution; it is most useful in fattening rations.
Ration formulas are the same family as for cows (cottonseed cake, maize gluten feed, wheat bran, rice polish, molasses, salt, DCP); ask for the cow formulas for exact percentages.
Dry off a high-yielding buffalo about two months before calving: first reduce feed so milk drops, then milk once a day instead of twice, emptying the udder fully; stopping suddenly risks mastitis. Then give good concentrate and quality green fodder for healthier calves, more milk and higher fat.
aspects.health:
Get a diagnosis from a Livestock Department lab or a qualified vet before any medicine, and vaccinate as the Livestock Department advises.
Vaccination schedule:
Haemorrhagic septicaemia (HS, gal ghotu): disease of low-lying areas, spreads in monsoon and winter rains and kills many cattle and buffaloes quickly. Signs: high fever, difficult breathing, swelling under the throat, bluish tongue, bloody dysentery; death from choking if treatment is late. Sulfa drugs work quickly. Vaccinate in May–June and November–December (twice a year, immunity six months).
Foot and mouth disease (FMD): virus, mostly in spring; high fever, blisters in the mouth and between the hooves, difficulty eating and walking, limping, less milk; few deaths in adults. Vaccinate twice a year (February–March or March–April, and August–October); immunity six months. Wash sores with potassium permanganate and use antibiotics as advised.
Black quarter (chorray maar): hot, painful, crackling swelling on the thigh or shoulder; limping. Vaccinate once a year in February–April; immunity one year.
Anthrax (goli, sut): high fever, restlessness, red swollen eyes, blood in dung and urine; often found dead, with unclotted blood from body openings. Vaccinate in August; immunity one year.
Lumpy skin disease: skin lumps, fever, watery eyes. Vaccinate, give painkiller and antibiotic as advised, control flies and mosquitoes.
Mastitis: germs enter the udder through unhygienic milking; can affect one to four teats; treat with antibiotics, or the teat or whole udder can be lost. Keep the shed clean, milk with the full hand (not the bent thumb), and test milk at a lab sometimes.
Rinderpest: Pakistan is now free of it.
Bloat (aphara): from irregular feeding or too much fresh berseem or shaftal; the left flank swells and breathing is hard; can kill. Give half a litre of mustard or linseed oil with 50 ml of turpentine oil. In emergencies a vet can use a trocar and cannula.
Impaction (stomach blockage): from poor, smelly or mouldy feed; the animal stops chewing cud, has pain and constipation. A laxative such as magnesium sulphate helps.
Milk fever: in high-yielding buffaloes about 48 hours after calving, from low calcium; no fever, the animal sits with its head turned to its chest, half-conscious. Calcium gluconate injection into the vein works well. Regular mineral mixture (or DCP and salt) prevents it; high vitamin D from 3 to 4 days before to 2 days after calving also helps.
Brucellosis: abortion at 5 to 7 months; vaccinate.
Buffaloes wallow in mud, which brings germs and parasites, so they are more prone to infections, including of the reproductive organs.
aspects.deworming:
External parasites (lice, ticks, mites) suck blood and weaken the animal: clip the hair and spray an approved parasiticide on the animal and in the shed.
Internal worms (liver and stomach flukes and worms) come from pastures and ponds and cause poor appetite, indigestion, constipation, weakness and diarrhoea, raising deaths. Spray pastures with a 2 percent copper sulphate (neela thotha) solution, and give dewormers every 4 months. Suckling calves get round and long worms that can kill them; dewormers such as Nilverm, Systemex, Oxafax and Zanil help, but consult a vet first. Dewormers such as albendazole or ivermectin are also used. Get dung tested at a lab and follow the vet.
aspects.milking: Missing even one feed or one day's timely water drops milk at the next milking, so keep fixed times for feeding and milking; changes upset the animals. Prepare buffaloes two hours before milking: clean the whole body, especially the udder, teats, legs and tail; a bath in a pond or canal works well. Use the same milker for the same animals; skilled, quick milkers get more milk in less time. Noise makes buffaloes hold back milk. The last streams of milk have up to 2.3 percent more fat. Use breeding dates to predict calving and dry off about two months before. If milk smells, add 20 g of baking soda to the fodder daily for one week. Keep all milking equipment, the milker and his clothes very clean.
aspects.other: Buffaloes supply about half of Pakistan's meat and much of its milk.
